title: Adaptive reasoning
subtitle: The capacity for logical thought, reflection, explanation, and justification — the glue that ties the other strands together.

sections.sources: Grounded in NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) & the five strands of mathematical proficiency.

blocks.text: Adaptive reasoning is the capacity for logical thought, reflection, explanation, and justification — the ability to think through a problem and say *why* an answer is right.

*Adding It Up* calls this strand the “glue that holds everything together.” It is how students decide whether a strategy is valid, whether a claim is always true, and how the pieces of their thinking connect. In 6–8 this shows up as informal argument and justification — the seedbed of proof.
What it looks like in a student

items: Justifies answers: “it works because…”, not “because I got it.”
Evaluates someone else's reasoning — agrees or disagrees with a mathematical reason.
Tests whether a pattern will *always* hold, not just for one case.
Reflects and revises when a step doesn't hold up.

blocks.text: Adaptive reasoning is what lets a student use conceptual understanding and fluency together and know that the result makes sense. Without it, the other strands stay separate and unexamined.
Instructional practices that build it — and how
These Effective Teaching Practices develop adaptive reasoning most directly:

rows: Justifying your own thinking and evaluating a classmate's is reasoning made public — the strand in action.
“How do you know? Will that always work?” is a direct, repeatable demand for justification.
Reflection and revision — the heart of reasoning — happen while students work through difficulty, not after they're told the answer.
Tasks worth arguing about give reasoning something real to chew on.

blocks.text: In the toolbelt, [Talk Moves](/math/approach/talk-moves), [Error Analysis](/math/approach/error-analysis), and [Same But Different / WODB](/math/approach/same-but-different) all demand justification, not just answers.

“Because I followed the steps” is not justification. If students only ever report answers and are never asked to defend or evaluate them, this strand goes undeveloped — no matter how accurate they are.
“How do you know? Will that always work?” Adaptive reasoning is the difference between an answer and an argument.
